---
title: 2 - Add a WMS layer
---


In this chapter, you will add a geospatial data layer to your webmap using a Web Map Service (WMS).

WMS delivers rendered map images from a remote geospatial server, such as **GeoServer**. Instead of downloading and displaying the original vector features in your browser, OpenLayers requests map images from the server for the area currently being viewed.

We will start from an existing OpenLayers example and adapt it to display conservation areas in Tanzania.



## 2.1. Start with an OpenLayers example

Open official OpenLayers example [Single Image WMS](https://openlayers.org/en/latest/examples/wms-image.html) that we will use as the base for our whole webmap.

This example demonstrates how to display a WMS layer in OpenLayers. Its original dataset covers US states, but we will replace that dataset with a layer served by the [Climate Risk Database](https://crd.resilienceacademy.ac.tz/). 

Review the `index.html` and `main.js` files in the example. Copy the code from these two files, and paste them into your corresponding `index.html` and `main.js` files.

Save the files (often Ctrl/Command + S) and refresh your localhost development server to see the changes on your webmap. At this stage, your map should be exactly as the [Single Image WMS](https://openlayers.org/en/latest/examples/wms-image.html) example.

*Screenshot 1: The original Single Image WMS example, showing the US states layer.*


## 2.2. Find the WMS service and layer

We will use **Tanzania World Heritage and Ramsar Sites 2026** dataset published via Climate Risk Database (CRD).

Open [Tanzania World Heritage and Ramsar Sites 2026](https://crd.resilienceacademy.ac.tz/catalogue/#/dataset/1102) in CRD --> Click **Open properties** --> **Copy OGC Web Services URL** --> Paste the link somewhere for you to edit, such as on a notepad or at the end of your `main.js` file (remember to delete later).

*Screenshot 2: The dataset or GeoServer page showing the layer name and the OGC service information.*



## 2.3. Replace the example layer

Open `main.js` and locate the existing WMS layer configuration. We will change the service URL, the layer name and the extent so that the map displays the Tanzanian dataset. 

Once located, examine the original code in `main.js` file where the WMS connection is created:

```javascript
new ImageLayer({
    extent: [-13884991, 2870341, -7455066, 6338219],
    source: new ImageWMS({
      url: 'https://ahocevar.com/geoserver/wms',
      params: {'LAYERS': 'topp:states'},
      ratio: 1,
      serverType: 'geoserver',
    }),
  }),
```

Then, examine the copied OGC Web Service link to our Tanzania-layer:

https://crd.resilienceacademy.ac.tz/geoserver/geonode/tanzania_international_conservation_areas_2026/ows

As you can see, all the required elements to create a WMS connection to this layer can be found from the link - it just needs to be pieced into correct sections:
* https://crd.resilienceacademy.ac.tz/geoserver/ - the address to the GeoServer where all layers in CRD are stored and published.
* geonode/tanzania_international_conservation_areas_2026/ - the GeoServer **workspace (geonode)** and name of the layer file
* ows - the standard how the layer is served via the web. Climate Risk Database automatically suggests to serve the layer through *any* web service (OWS standard), but for our webmap, we can define that we use the WMS standard, meaning that we use the existing visualisation, and in an image format that is light-weight for a webmap to display.
### Starting point


### Edit the code

Edit your `main.js` file to create a connection to the Tanzania World Heritage and Ramsar Sites 2026 layer, instead of the US States layer by replacing the `url` and `params` parameters in the section where a WMS layer is configured.

Now, the code should look like this:

`main.js`
```javascript
new ImageLayer({
    extent: [-13884991, 2870341, -7455066, 6338219],
    source: new ImageWMS({
      url: 'https://crd.resilienceacademy.ac.tz/geoserver/wms',
      params: {'LAYERS': 'geonode:tanzania_international_conservation_areas_2026'},
      ratio: 1,
      serverType: 'geoserver',
    }),
  }),
```

Change the `extent` parameter coordinates to match extent of Tanzania. Often, these coordinates can be extracted from GeoServer, or approximated e.g. in Google Maps or QGIS. The coordinates represent the top-left and bottom-right corner of a bounding box that covers the data layer.

`extent: [3228700, -1381359, 4567834, -162868]`

The extent must use the same coordinate reference system as the map view. Default coordniate system of OpenLayers webmaps is WGS84, and fortunately, the layer is in the same CRS.

*Screenshot 3: The map after replacing the WMS source, before adjusting the map view. If the layer is outside the current extent, explain this in the caption.*

Save `main.js` and refresh your local webmap.

At this stage, the map may still be centred on the United States. The US states layer should no longer be displayed, and the Tanzanian layer may be outside the current map view. This is expected. In the next chapter, you will adjust the map's initial centre and zoom level to bring Tanzania into view.


### Checkpoint

Before continuing, confirm that:

- The original US states layer configuration has been replaced.
- The WMS service URL and layer name are correct.
- The application runs without JavaScript errors.

If the layer does not appear later when you centre the map on Tanzania, check the service URL, layer name, extent and browser developer console.
